title: The rule that doesn't mention anyone
subtitle: Indirect discrimination and the s 19 PCP test
objectives: State the four elements of the s 19 Equality Act 2010 test for indirect discrimination
Distinguish group disadvantage from individual disadvantage and explain why both must be shown
Apply the objective justification defence — legitimate aim and proportionate means — to a new fact pattern

leadingAuthorities.role: Defines indirect discrimination: a provision, criterion or practice (PCP) applied equally that disadvantages a protected group
Confirms no need to show why the PCP disadvantages the group — only that it does — and separates group disadvantage from individual causation

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Students who did well on direct discrimination (Lesson 9) often assume indirect discrimination is the same test with a different name. It isn't — it doesn't ask about anyone's intentions or even anyone's awareness. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You know the four elements — this lesson checks whether you can find a PCP hiding inside a fact pattern that never uses the word.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below leans on scenarios: spotting the PCP and running the justification defence, not reciting the section.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and be precise about the four elements in order — PCP, applies to everyone, particular disadvantage to the group, and disadvantage to this claimant. Skipping one is the most common way to lose marks in this area.

overview.hook: No one in this lesson's leading case was ever treated worse than a colleague because of a protected characteristic — not on the face of it. Every employee sat the same test, worked the same shift pattern, cleared the same promotion bar as everyone else. And yet the Supreme Court found unlawful discrimination anyway. That's the whole point of indirect discrimination: it doesn't need anyone to single you out. It just needs a rule that looks neutral and lands unevenly.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 24 September 2026. The s 19 Equality Act 2010 test itself is stable, but the Employment Rights Act 2025's phased reforms (see Lesson 15) are altering the wider unfair dismissal landscape this discrimination law sits alongside; nothing in the ERA 2025 currently changes s 19 itself.

parts.heading: A rule for everyone that isn't neutral at all
parts.voice: argumentative — sets up why the law needed a second discrimination test at all
body: Direct discrimination, from Lesson 9, is about treatment that turns on a protected characteristic — someone is treated worse *because of* their race, sex, disability, and so on. But plenty of genuinely harmful discrimination never mentions a protected characteristic anywhere in the rule. A requirement that all applicants be over six feet tall doesn't name a sex. A rule that everyone must work full time, with no exceptions, doesn't name a sex either. Both, in practice, screen out disproportionately more women than men.

Indirect discrimination, under s 19 Equality Act 2010, exists to catch exactly this: a facially neutral rule, applied identically to everyone, that nonetheless puts people who share a protected characteristic at a particular disadvantage compared with people who don't. Crucially, the employer doesn't need to have intended anything by it, and may not even have realised the rule had that effect. Motive is irrelevant to liability — it only ever surfaces later, in the justification defence.

This is a harder test to spot in an exam than direct discrimination, precisely because the facts won't flag it for you. There's no comparator moment where someone was treated differently from a colleague. Instead you're looking for a rule, requirement, or practice — applied uniformly — and then asking who, statistically or practically, struggles to meet it.

components.definition: Any rule, requirement, policy or way of doing things applied by an employer — a shift pattern, a qualification requirement, an appraisal criterion, an unwritten custom. It need not be formal or written down; a one-off decision can, in limited circumstances, also count as a practice.

interaction.prompt: An employer requires all warehouse staff to be able to lift 25kg unaided, applying this equally to every applicant regardless of sex. Could this still amount to indirect discrimination?
options: Yes — a rule applied identically to everyone can still be indirect discrimination if it disadvantages a protected group
No — treating everyone identically can never amount to discrimination
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Identical treatment is exactly the fact pattern s 19 is built for — the question is not whether the rule is applied evenly, but who it disadvantages once applied.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — identical treatment is the starting point for indirect discrimination, not a defence to it. The question s 19 asks is what a neutral-looking rule actually does to a protected group in practice.

parts.heading: The four elements of s 19
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: Section 19 sets out a precise, four-stage test. Miss a stage and you're either arguing the wrong point or skipping a step an examiner is watching for.

First, there must be a PCP. Second, A applies (or would apply) it to persons who do not share B's protected characteristic. Third — the core of the test — the PCP puts, or would put, persons who share B's characteristic at a particular disadvantage compared with persons who don't share it. Fourth, it puts, or would put, B specifically at that disadvantage. And even if all four are shown, the employer has one route back out: showing the PCP is a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim.
Notice the test is prospective as well as retrospective — 'puts, or would put' — so a claimant doesn't need to wait for the disadvantage to actually bite before challenging the PCP.

components.text: (1) A person (A) discriminates against another (B) if A applies to B a provision, criterion or practice which is discriminatory in relation to a relevant protected characteristic of B's. (2) For the purposes of subsection (1), a provision, criterion or practice is discriminatory in relation to a relevant protected characteristic of B's if — (a) A applies, or would apply, it to persons with whom B does not share the characteristic, (b) it puts, or would put, persons with whom B shares the characteristic at a particular disadvantage when compared with persons with whom B does not share it, (c) it puts, or would put, B at that disadvantage, and (d) A cannot show it to be a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim.
elements: A PCP exists and is applied, or would be applied, to everyone regardless of the characteristic
It puts, or would put, people sharing B's characteristic at a particular disadvantage compared with those who don't
It puts, or would put, B specifically at that disadvantage
A cannot show the PCP is a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim

components.label: The four elements in order
points: 1. Identify the PCP — the neutral rule or practice in play
2. It's applied (or would be applied) to everyone regardless of the protected characteristic
3. Group disadvantage — people sharing B's characteristic are put at a particular disadvantage compared with those who don't
4. Individual disadvantage — B personally is put at that disadvantage too
Defence — the employer can still escape liability by showing objective justification

interaction.prompt: Put these four elements of the s 19 test in the order the section sets them out.
items: A applies a PCP equally to everyone
The PCP puts B's protected group at a particular disadvantage compared with others
The PCP puts B personally at that disadvantage
A fails to show the PCP is a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the statutory sequence: apply the PCP evenly, show group disadvantage, show individual disadvantage, then see whether justification saves it.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again — s 19 moves from the PCP itself, to disadvantage for the group, to disadvantage for this claimant, and only then to the justification defence.

parts.heading: Essop: disadvantage without an explanation
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells the story before naming the doctrine
body: Essop v Home Office concerns Home Office staff, including UK Border Agency staff, who had to pass a Core Skills Assessment to be eligible for promotion. Statistical evidence showed that candidates from black and minority ethnic backgrounds, and older candidates, passed the assessment at a materially lower rate than white and younger candidates. Mr Essop, who was both, failed the assessment and was refused promotion.

The Home Office argued the claim should fail because nobody — including its own experts — could explain *why* the assessment produced this pattern. No one had identified a specific feature of the test that caused the disparity. The Court of Appeal had accepted that argument. The Supreme Court reversed it.

Lord Nash, giving the leading judgment, held that s 19 does not require a claimant to prove the reason for the group disadvantage — only that the PCP in fact causes it, and that it in fact disadvantaged this claimant. Requiring proof of a causal mechanism would make many genuine indirect discrimination claims impossible to bring, since disparate impact can be real and statistically robust without anyone being able to say precisely why a test or practice operates unevenly.

components.factsShort: BME and older Home Office staff passed a promotion assessment at a lower rate than others, with no identified reason why.
components.ratioShort: A claimant need not prove why a PCP causes group disadvantage — only that it does, and that it disadvantaged them personally.

expanded.facts: The Core Skills Assessment was a pass/fail test used by the Home Office as a gateway to promotion within certain grades. Statistical pooling of results across many sittings showed BME candidates and older candidates passed at a significantly lower rate than white and younger candidates, but no expert on either side could identify what feature of the test caused this. Mr Essop, one of the affected employees, brought an indirect discrimination claim after repeated failure blocked his promotion.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Supreme Court held that s 19 has no requirement that the claimant explain the reason for the disparity — it is enough that the PCP puts the group at a disadvantage in fact, and that the individual claimant shares in that disadvantage. The court also clarified that the disadvantage suffered by the individual need not be caused in exactly the same way as the group disadvantage generally, so long as it is the same PCP producing both.
expanded.significance: Essop is the leading modern authority separating the 'why' from the 'what' in indirect discrimination: claimants must show a PCP causes group and individual disadvantage, but not the mechanism by which it does so. This makes indirect discrimination genuinely easier to establish on the facts than direct discrimination, where a reason for the treatment usually has to be identified.

interaction.prompt: What did the Supreme Court in Essop hold a claimant does NOT need to prove?
options: That the PCP disadvantaged the claimant personally
That the PCP disadvantaged the claimant's protected group
Why the PCP causes the group disadvantage
That the employer applied the PCP to everyone regardless of the characteristic
interaction.trapExplanation: It's tempting to think a causal explanation is always required in discrimination law, because direct discrimination usually turns on identifying a reason for the treatment. Essop holds the opposite for indirect discrimination: the 'why' is irrelevant to liability — only the statistical or practical fact of disadvantage, at group and individual level, needs to be shown.

parts.heading: Group disadvantage and individual disadvantage are two different hurdles
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the puzzle before resolving it
body: Here's a question that trips up even strong students: if a PCP disadvantages women as a group, does every woman affected by it automatically have a claim? No — and this is where s 19(2)(c) does real, independent work.

Take a PCP requiring all staff to work full time. Suppose the evidence shows this disadvantages women generally, because women are statistically more likely to have caring responsibilities that make full-time work harder. A woman who is refused flexible working under that PCP, and who does have caring responsibilities that the rule genuinely burdens, clears both hurdles — group disadvantage and individual disadvantage. But a woman who is affected by the same PCP for reasons entirely unconnected to caring responsibilities — she simply prefers part-time work for hobbies, say — has not personally suffered the disadvantage the PCP is shown to cause the group. She may still be inconvenienced by the rule, but that isn't enough; s 19(2)(c) requires the PCP to put *her* at *that* disadvantage, not just any disadvantage.

This is why group and individual disadvantage are pleaded, and assessed, separately. Statistical or cohort evidence typically proves the group stage; the claimant's own facts prove the individual stage. Both must be established — one without the other fails the test.

components.title: Group disadvantage vs individual disadvantage
components.description: How the two disadvantage requirements in s 19 relate to each other.

nodes.label: Does the PCP put B's protected group at a particular disadvantage vs others? (usually statistical/cohort evidence)
Yes → does the PCP put B personally at that same disadvantage? (B's own facts)
No → claim fails at s 19(2)(c), even though group disadvantage is proven
Yes → both hurdles cleared; employer may still raise objective justification

components.textAlternative: After identifying the PCP, first ask whether it disadvantages B's protected group as a whole, usually using statistical or cohort evidence. If not, the claim fails at that stage. If it does, separately ask whether the PCP puts B personally at that same disadvantage, using B's own facts. If B is not personally affected in that way, the claim fails even though group disadvantage was proven. Only if both hurdles are cleared does the analysis move to the employer's objective justification defence.

interaction.prompt: A supermarket requires all shift supervisors to be available for the 5am starts. Evidence shows this disadvantages employees with school-age children generally. Which employee has the stronger individual disadvantage claim under s 19(2)(c)?
interaction.scenarioA: Nadia has a seven-year-old with no other carer available before 8am, and cannot take the 5am shift as a result.
interaction.scenarioB: Priya has no caring responsibilities at all but personally dislikes early mornings and would rather not work them.
interaction.explanation: Nadia's difficulty tracks the exact disadvantage the group evidence identifies — caring responsibilities colliding with a 5am start. Priya's preference isn't connected to the disadvantage the PCP is shown to cause the group, so even though the PCP inconveniences her too, s 19(2)(c) isn't satisfied on these facts.

parts.heading: The only way out: objective justification
parts.voice: direct — sets up the defence students will be tested on hardest
body: If all four elements of s 19(2) are made out, the employer isn't automatically liable. Section 19(2)(d) gives a single defence: the employer can escape liability by showing the PCP is a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim. This is often called the 'objective justification' defence, and unlike direct discrimination — which (age aside) has almost no general justification defence — indirect discrimination is justifiable in principle for any protected characteristic.

Two things must both be shown, and tribunals treat each seriously. A legitimate aim is a real business need — not merely a preference or administrative convenience dressed up in a serious-sounding label, and never an aim that is itself discriminatory (cost alone, for example, is not a legitimate aim, though cost combined with another genuine business reason can be). Proportionate means requires the employer to show the PCP is an appropriate and reasonably necessary way of achieving that aim — and, critically, that no less discriminatory alternative would achieve the same aim. A PCP that goes further than necessary, when a milder rule would do the same job, fails at proportionality even where the underlying aim is entirely legitimate.

This is where fact patterns are won and lost in application questions. Students who identify the PCP and the disadvantage correctly often lose marks by treating 'the employer had a reason' as the end of the analysis — a reason is not the same as a legitimate aim pursued by proportionate means, and an examiner will usually build in a less discriminatory alternative the employer never considered.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often conclude a PCP is justified because the employer 'had a good business reason' for it, treating any rational explanation as sufficient.
components.whyItsWrong: Objective justification is a two-part, objective test applied by the tribunal, not a subjective assessment of whether the employer's reasoning was sincere or sensible-sounding. A rational-sounding aim can still fail if it's not genuinely a business necessity, and even a genuine aim fails if the PCP goes further than proportionate — especially where a less discriminatory alternative existed and was never explored.

interaction.prompt: An employer requires all managers to have five years' continuous full-time experience, shown to disadvantage women who took career breaks for childcare. The employer's only stated reason is that it's 'always been the rule.' How confident are you this PCP would survive objective justification?
interaction.explanation: 'It's always been the rule' is not a legitimate aim — it identifies no business necessity at all, let alone a proportionate one. Without evidence of a genuine need for continuous full-time experience specifically (rather than, say, five years' experience in any pattern), this PCP is very unlikely to be justified.

testPool.prompt: Name the statutory provision that defines indirect discrimination and give its core requirement in one sentence.
acceptableAnswers: s 19 Equality Act 2010 — a PCP applied equally that disadvantages a protected group
section 19, a neutral rule applied to everyone that puts a protected group at a particular disadvantage
testPool.modelAnswer: Section 19 Equality Act 2010: a provision, criterion or practice applied equally to everyone that puts people sharing a protected characteristic at a particular disadvantage compared with others, and puts the claimant at that disadvantage too, unless the employer shows it is a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim.

testPool.prompt: Does an employer need to have intended to disadvantage a protected group to be liable under s 19?
options: No — intention is irrelevant to liability under s 19
Yes — indirect discrimination requires proof of intent

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the four elements a claimant must prove under s 19(2)?
options: A PCP applied, or that would be applied, to persons who don't share B's characteristic
The PCP puts B's protected group at a particular disadvantage compared with others
The employer intended to discriminate against B
The PCP puts B personally at that disadvantage
testPool.trapExplanation: Intent has no place in s 19(2) at all — the four statutory elements are the PCP, its equal application, group disadvantage and individual disadvantage, with justification as the employer's defence. Reading in an intent requirement confuses indirect discrimination with the state of mind sometimes relevant to direct discrimination.

testPool.prompt: Under s 19(2)(d), what must an employer show to escape liability once the other three elements are made out?
options: That the PCP is a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim
That the claimant suffered no financial loss
That other employees of the same protected characteristic were unaffected

testPool.prompt: Order the reasoning steps a tribunal follows when assessing a s 19 claim.
items: Identify the PCP and confirm it is applied equally to everyone
Assess whether the PCP puts the claimant's protected group at a particular disadvantage
Assess whether the PCP puts the claimant personally at that disadvantage
Consider whether the employer can show objective justification

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, drawn from the reasoning in Essop, highlight the sentence stating the ratio on causation.
testPool.passage: The Core Skills Assessment was applied identically to all candidates seeking promotion. Statistical evidence showed BME and older candidates passed at a lower rate, though no expert could identify the specific feature of the test responsible. It is not necessary for a claimant to establish the reason for the disparity; it is enough that the PCP in fact causes the group to suffer a disadvantage, and that the claimant shares in it.
testPool.ratioSentence: It is not necessary for a claimant to establish the reason for the disparity; it is enough that the PCP in fact causes the group to suffer a disadvantage, and that the claimant shares in it.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario that identifies the PCP.
testPool.scenarioText: A law firm requires all trainees to attend an unpaid networking breakfast every Friday at 7am as an informal condition of being considered for a training contract offer. Several part-time trainees with childcare commitments cannot attend and are consistently overlooked for offers.
tappableSpans: an unpaid networking breakfast every Friday at 7am
several part-time trainees with childcare commitments
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Right — the requirement (applied to everyone) that trainees attend the 7am breakfast is the PCP. The other facts describe its content, who it disadvantages, and the disadvantage itself, but the requirement is the rule doing the work.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the rule or requirement being applied to everyone — that's the PCP. The other facts describe the timing, who it affects, and the consequence, but the PCP is the requirement itself.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario better satisfies the individual disadvantage requirement in s 19(2)(c)?
testPool.scenarioA: A PCP requiring evening availability is shown to disadvantage Muslim employees generally due to prayer-time conflicts; Aisha, a Muslim employee, is refused a role after declining evening shifts specifically because of prayer commitments that clash with them.
testPool.scenarioB: The same PCP exists, and Aisha is refused the same role, but purely because she has a second job in the evenings unconnected to any religious observance.
testPool.explanation: In A, Aisha's personal disadvantage tracks the exact disadvantage shown at group level — prayer-time conflict with evening shifts. In B, although Aisha is a Muslim employee affected by the same PCP, her disadvantage arises from an unrelated cause, so s 19(2)(c) is not satisfied even though the group-level evidence in A would still apply generally.

testPool.prompt: A call centre requires all staff to work a rotating shift pattern including some night shifts, with no exceptions. Evidence shows this disadvantages employees with disabilities that make night work medically inadvisable. Ade, who has such a disability, is dismissed for refusing night shifts. Which s 19 element is most clearly satisfied by Ade's dismissal specifically?
options: Individual disadvantage under s 19(2)(c)
Group disadvantage under s 19(2)(b)
Equal application under s 19(2)(a)
testPool.explanation: Ade's own dismissal, caused by his own medical inability to work nights, is the individual disadvantage limb — it's his personal facts showing he shares in the group disadvantage already established by the wider medical evidence.

testPool.prompt: A hospital requires all surgeons to be available for 24-hour on-call rotations, citing patient safety as its reason, and offers no exceptions or flexible alternatives despite evidence that a modified rota covering the same on-call hours across a larger pool of surgeons would achieve identical safety outcomes. Is the PCP likely to be objectively justified?
options: No — a genuine and legitimate aim exists, but the PCP is not proportionate because a less discriminatory alternative achieving the same aim was available and not adopted
Yes — patient safety is always a sufficient justification for any PCP
No — patient safety can never be a legitimate aim in employment law
testPool.explanation: Patient safety is a paradigm example of a legitimate aim, so the PCP doesn't fail at that stage. But proportionality requires the employer to use the least discriminatory means reasonably available, and the existence of an equally effective, less restrictive rota defeats justification here.

testPool.prompt: Can indirect discrimination based on age be objectively justified in the same way as indirect discrimination based on sex or race?
options: Yes — the s 19(2)(d) justification defence applies to all protected characteristics, including age
No — age is the only characteristic where indirect discrimination can never be justified

testPool.prompt: An accountancy firm requires all associates seeking promotion to partner to have billed a minimum of 2,000 chargeable hours per year for five consecutive years, with no allowance for periods of part-time work. Statistical evidence across the firm shows women are promoted to partner at roughly half the rate of men, correlating closely with periods of part-time working after maternity leave. Farida, an associate who worked part-time for eighteen months after having a child, falls short of the five consecutive full years and is refused promotion. Analyse whether the firm's PCP amounts to unlawful indirect discrimination.
factsToOrder: The 2,000-hour, five-consecutive-year rule is applied to every associate seeking promotion
Firm-wide data shows women are promoted at roughly half the rate of men
The disparity correlates with periods of part-time working after maternity leave
Farida worked part-time for eighteen months after childbirth and fell short of the five consecutive years
Farida is refused promotion as a result

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the five-consecutive-year, 2,000-hour rule amounts to indirect sex discrimination against Farida under s 19 Equality Act 2010.
modelAnswer.rule: Section 19 requires a PCP applied equally to everyone, which puts the claimant's protected group at a particular disadvantage compared with others, puts the claimant personally at that disadvantage, and which the employer cannot show to be a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim (Essop v Home Office on causation).
modelAnswer.application: The PCP — the hours-and-continuity requirement — is applied to every associate regardless of sex, satisfying s 19(2)(a). The firm-wide statistics linking the promotion gap to part-time working after maternity leave establish group disadvantage to women under s 19(2)(b), and, following Essop, no further explanation of the mechanism is required. Farida's own facts — part-time work after childbirth causing her to fall short of continuous full years — show she personally shares in that disadvantage, satisfying s 19(2)(c). The firm would need to show a legitimate aim (such as ensuring partners have sufficient client-facing experience) pursued by proportionate means; a rigid rule with no allowance for part-time periods, when a pro-rated or extended qualifying period could achieve the same aim, is likely to fail proportionality.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The PCP is very likely to amount to unlawful indirect discrimination against Farida, since the firm has a plausible legitimate aim but the rigidity of the rule — with no less discriminatory alternative considered — makes objective justification difficult to sustain.

testPool.prompt: An employer argues a PCP is justified purely because implementing an alternative would cost more money. On the authorities, is cost alone a legitimate aim?
sliderLabels: Cost alone is never a legitimate aim
testPool.correctPosition: Cost alone is never a legitimate aim
testPool.explanation: Students often round this off to one extreme or the other. The accurate position sits in between: 'cost alone' is not accepted as a legitimate aim by itself, but cost is not irrelevant either — it can properly form part of a wider justification alongside a genuine, independent business reason.

testPool.prompt: Name the leading case establishing that a claimant need not prove why a PCP causes group disadvantage under s 19.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is stopping the analysis once a PCP and some disadvantage are identified. Group disadvantage, individual disadvantage, and objective justification are three separate hurdles — an answer that blends them together, or skips straight to 'the employer had a reason,' loses marks even when the PCP is correctly spotted.
